name: Heatmap Calendar
summary: Half a year of daily values in one block, navigable by day and by week from the keyboard, with every cell carrying its own date and count as a label.

attempts.prompt: Build a contribution-graph style heatmap calendar.
attempts.problem: A grid of divs with five background colours and a title attribute on each. Title tooltips do not appear on keyboard focus and are not read by most screen readers, so every value in the chart was invisible to anyone not using a mouse. Nothing was focusable at all, so the component was a picture.

attempts.prompt: Make the cells focusable and readable by assistive technology.
attempts.problem: Made all 182 cells tabbable, which puts 182 stops between the heatmap and the next control on the page. Arrow keys were mapped as though DOM order were rows, so Left and Right moved by one day while Up and Down jumped a week — the opposite of what the layout shows, because the grid flows down each week column.

finalPrompt:
Build a heatmap calendar in plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no dependencies, showing about 26 weeks of daily values.

Lay it out with grid-auto-flow: column and seven rows, so each column is one week running Sunday to Saturday.

That layout choice has a consequence the keyboard handling must respect: DOM order runs down each week, so moving one day is plus or minus 1 in the DOM while moving one week is plus or minus 7. Map Arrow Down and Up to a day, Arrow Right and Left to a week, and Home and End to the first and last day of the current week. Getting this backwards makes the component feel broken in a way that is hard to name.

Use a roving tabindex: exactly one cell is tabbable and the arrow keys move it. Never make every cell tabbable — 182 tab stops before the next control is not navigation.

Every cell is a real button with an aria-label stating the count and the formatted date, and the grid carries role="grid" with cells as role="gridcell". Do not use the title attribute for values: it does not appear on keyboard focus and most screen readers ignore it, which makes the entire chart invisible to anyone not using a mouse.

Mirror the focused cell's label into a role="status" region so sighted keyboard users see the value too.

Five intensity levels, expressed as color-mix of the accent into the empty-cell background, so the ramp is one hue at increasing strength rather than five arbitrary colours.

Format dates with Intl.DateTimeFormat and no locale argument, so it follows the user's locale rather than assuming one.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--raised), var(--accent), var(--text), var(--text-dim). No literal hex, rgb or hsl values.
why:
The axis-mapping bug is the one worth keeping. The layout is columns, so the DOM neighbour is the next day and the element seven away is the next week — but the visual neighbour to the right is a week later. A model writing arrow handling reaches for the familiar rows mapping and produces a grid where the keys fight the picture. Stating the consequence explicitly, as a property of the chosen layout, is what fixed it.

The title-attribute point generalises: title is not an accessibility mechanism. It is invisible to keyboards, inconsistent across screen readers, and unusable on touch. Any time a value lives only in a tooltip, the chart has no data for a large share of its users.

And the roving tabindex is the standard answer for any grid of many controls, for the simple reason that a hundred tab stops is not navigation.
